prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which brought the measurement of time and frequency with neutral atoms to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B024 as the whole prize, and my confidence has gone up a little, because the objections raised against it are about lineage and bookkeeping, not about the physics. The lattice clock is a new measurement capability: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping lets thousands of atoms be interrogated without Doppler, recoil or first-order light shifts, and the Ye group's work took that to a systematic uncertainty near 1e-18, which several independent laboratories have since reproduced and compared clock to clock. That is exactly the kind of result that widens what can be measured, and it has already enabled relativistic time-dilation tests over centimetre height differences, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and chronometric geodesy. The credit is two names, a proposer-and-first-demonstrator and the group that set the record performance, and it is the only credit on the shortlist that three or more members have independently called the cleanest. I also note that B024 is the listed fallback of Eriksson, Olsson and Mehlig, so it is the one configuration that nearly the whole committee can live with. I take the performance figures and priority history from recollection, and I support the request for a short expert check before the final ballot.
statement.case_against: The lineage objection is still the most serious one: the 2005 prize (frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (control of single quantum systems) honoured the enabling tools, so a sceptic can read the lattice clock as an excellent instrument on honoured foundations. I answer that the clock is a distinct regime and not a repeat, but I accept that nobody has yet set the two earlier citations side by side with this one, and that is a weakness in our own argument. The credit also leaves out serious contributors (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, the Sr and Yb clock groups, Takamoto and Ludlow), and the formal redefinition of the second has not happened. If the committee believes a prize should follow the redefinition, the case is weaker this year, though I would not call it disqualifying since the demonstrated performance does not depend on the redefinition.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B020 because a simple quantitative theory (Bistritzer-MacDonald 2011) preceded an unexpected experimental discovery in twisted bilayer graphene, and says that if the committee wants a settled mechanism, B024 is the honest fallback.
responses.response: I agree that prediction followed by unexpected discovery is the strongest kind of case, and I do not dismiss B020; I rank it first among my alternatives. My difficulty is the one you state yourself: a citation worded around observed phases rather than an explanation, eight years after the experiments, with twist-angle disorder still limiting quantitative reproducibility. As an experimentalist I would want the reproducibility of the phase diagram across devices to be tighter before I fix credit. The clock result is the opposite case: the central quantity, fractional frequency uncertainty, is reproduced by several laboratories with agreeing comparisons, so there is little interpretive room. You asked what evidence would make B024 distinct from earlier prizes; the answer I offer is the capability argument, namely many neutral atoms at once with recoil- and Doppler-free interrogation, which neither the comb nor single-ion control provides.

responses.point: Olsson supports B020 as a chain from falsifiable prediction to the original 2018 experiment, but says that if the committee cannot be sure the credited people did the original work, B024 is better documented, and she ranks B019 eighth and calls Halzen's credit fragile.
responses.response: Your conditional is where I think we meet. Your own test, that credit must be certain, is one B024 passes better than B020, since Yuan Cao, earlier moire band-structure theory and the hBN-device work all sit outside your three names, whereas for the clocks the disputed contributions are largely in the tail of independent reproductions and not in the original concept and the record-accuracy demonstration. I also agree with you on B019 and the single Halzen credit, and that is why I would not accept it as a second part. I would be glad to see B024 as a joint first choice for you, and I would ask whether you would prefer B020 to wait until the pairing mechanism and reproducibility are clearer, which would let it come back as a stronger single prize in a later year.

responses.point: Pearce proposes B024 plus B019 (Halzen alone) as two distinct instrument-led breakthroughs, and says the configuration should shrink to B024 alone if a one-name IceCube credit cannot be defended.
responses.response: I share your scientific ranking of B024 and your fallback rule, but I do not want to pair it with B019 in this round. My reasons are practical. The single Halzen credit for a detector built and analysed by hundreds is, as you say, fragile, and the shortlist offers no supportable way to add names. Adding a second part only to reach two achievements also weakens a clean B024 citation by making the committee defend two uneven credits. I agree with your point that a split prize would dilute B024, and I would ask you to confirm that you would vote for B024 alone if B019 does not hold.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the IceCube discovery first because a detection of nature is concrete, but concedes a single-name credit is awkward and notes there is room for two more names in a three-laureate prize.
responses.response: I accept your principle that discoveries of nature carry weight, and I do not question the IceCube detection. I would only say that the clock is also an experimental finding, in that a measurement of unprecedented precision is a result about nature, as the comparison of clocks at different heights shows. On the attribution, I think the open slot is a reason for caution and not for a fix: a third name added only to fill the quota would have to be justified for the discovery, and nobody has proposed one that the shortlist supports. If a defensible IceCube attribution emerges, I would be willing to look at it in a future year; for this vote I cannot support a configuration whose credit we cannot defend.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; no one has yet compared the citation texts.
Whether the priority history and the contributions of SYRTE, PTB and NIST, which I know only from recollection, would change the credited set if checked.
Whether recognising lattice clocks before the formal redefinition of the second is seen as timely or premature; I lean toward timely since the performance is already demonstrated.
The 1e-18 figures and the clock-to-clock agreement are from my own memory and should be checked against the record.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. Jun Ye trained in John Hall's group at JILA and I spent a year in Hall's laboratory during my PhD, so I have a distant personal and scientific link to the Hall-Ye lineage; I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye. My WACQT leadership role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, where Goran Johansson is based, which concerns B042 and not my preferred configuration. I have no objection to the committee ruling on Johansson's recusal for B042, and I would accept a ruling on my own Hall link if members think it matters.
